title: Butcher on a glm with a data.frame that has a single column
description:
Hey!

## The problem

I'm having trouble using butcher on a glm with a data.frame that has a single column:
> Error in is_scalar_vector(x) && is.na(x) :

```r
library(butcher)

model <- glm(y ~1, data = df)
```

title: Consider a different style of butchering for use cases that prioritize size of model object
description:
In rstudio/vetiver-r#264 @lschneiderbauer pointed out for their use case, they would like to remove more components. They don't need the components used for prediction/confidence intervals, and do need the model object to be smaller. They would like something along these lines:

``` r
library(butcher)
library(vetiver)

more_cars <- mtcars[rep(1:32, each = 1e4),]
cars_lm <- lm(mpg ~ ., data = more_cars)
weigh(cars_lm)
#> # A tibble: 25 × 2
#>    object         size
#>    <chr>         <dbl>
#>  1 qr.qr         54.0 
#>  2 residuals     28.4 
#>  3 fitted.values 28.4 
#>  4 effects        5.12
#>  5 model.mpg      2.56
#>  6 model.cyl      2.56
#>  7 model.disp     2.56
#>  8 model.hp       2.56
#>  9 model.drat     2.56
#> 10 model.wt       2.56
#> # ℹ 15 more rows

axe_custom <- function(x) {
    old <- x
    x <- butcher:::exchange(x, "residuals", numeric(0))
    x$qr <- butcher:::exchange(x$qr, "qr", matrix(0))
    x
}

axed_lm <- axe_custom(cars_lm)
weigh(axed_lm)
#> # A tibble: 25 × 2
#>    object         size
#>    <chr>         <dbl>
#>  1 fitted.values 28.4 
#>  2 effects        5.12
#>  3 model.mpg      2.56

#>  9 model.qsec     2.56
#> 10 model.vs       2.56
#> # ℹ 15 more rows

v <- vetiver_model(axed_lm, "custom-butchered-lm")
weigh(v)
#> # A tibble: 37 × 2
#>    object            size
#>    <chr>            <dbl>
#>  1 model.effects     5.12
#>  2 model.model.mpg   2.56
#>  3 model.model.cyl   2.56
#>  4 model.model.disp  2.56
#>  5 model.model.hp    2.56
#>  6 model.model.drat  2.56
#>  7 model.model.wt    2.56
#>  8 model.model.qsec  2.56
#>  9 model.model.vs    2.56

#> # ℹ 27 more rows
```

title: Can't predict on newdata when model formula includes poly()
description:
Thanks for developing this useful package!

## The problem

When I include a `poly(...)` in a model formula, then `butcher()` the model object, predicting on newdata using that butchered model object does not work. I've  had this problem with `lm` and `glm` model objects.

```r
m <- lm(speed ~ poly(dist, 2, raw =  TRUE), data = cars)
p0 <- predict(m, newdata = cars) # this works
mb <- butcher::butcher(m)
p1 <- predict(mb, newdata = cars) # this doesn't
# Error in poly(dist, 2, raw = TRUE) : could not find function "poly"
```

``` r
## note that `bart()` has a pretty nasty namespace collision:

set.seed(502)
ames_split <- ames |> 
    mutate(Sale_Price = log10(Sale_Price)) |> 
    initial_split(prop = 0.80, strata = Sale_Price)

ames_test  <- testing(ames_split)

ames_rec <- 
    recipe(Sale_Price ~ Neighborhood + Gr_Liv_Area + Year_Built + Bldg_Type +

    step_log(Gr_Liv_Area, base = 10) |>

    step_ns(Latitude, Longitude, deg_free = 20)


bart_model <- bart(mode = "regression")
bart_wflow <- workflow(ames_rec, bart_model)
fitted <- bart_wflow |> last_fit(ames_split) |> extract_workflow()
predict(fitted, new_data = slice_sample(ames_test, n = 1))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
```

title: Problems with `survival::coxph()` and env handling
description:
## perhaps reporting if any changes are made, even if overall object size is unchanged?

(thank you for a wonderful package and apologies if any of the below is due to my own misunderstandings!)

It seems to me that verbose = TRUE reports an unsuccessful `butcher` if the total memory of an object does not change, even though aspects of the object may successfully be butchered (I will admit to having only a very fuzzy understanding of memory).

I was confused by output when I ran into this situation and initially thought that `butcher` was not able to trim my coxph object:

``` r
library(tibble)
library(lobstr)
library(survival)
library(butcher)

example_data <-
  tibble::tibble(
    time = rpois(10000, 2) + 1,
    status = rbinom(10000, 1, .5),
    x = rpois(10000, .5),
    covar = rbinom(10000, 1, .5)
  )

coxph_formula <- function(data) {
  res <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x + strata(covar), data)
  res_formula <- res$formula
}

coxph_formula_butchered <- function(data) {
  res <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x + strata(covar), data)
  cleaned_res <- butcher(res, verbose = TRUE)
  res_formula <- cleaned_res$formula
}

res <- coxph_formula(example_data)
res_butchered <- coxph_formula_butchered(example_data)
#> ✖ No memory released. Do not butcher.

lobstr::obj_size(res)
#> 534.84 kB
lobstr::obj_size(res_butchered)
#> 1.49 kB
```

<sup>Created on 2023-04-23 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

but clearly the formula object is much reduced. I am assuming that the env (or the contents of the env) that is removed from `formula` exists in a different object, so the total size of `res_butchered` is unchanged and thus `assess_object` determines that nothing net changed. But would it be possible to report `memory_released` on the level of the implemented `axe` s as well as the overall object size?

(The message changes to the expected information about memory being released if only I had butchered the thing I was truly interested in (`res_formula <- butcher(res$formula, verbose = TRUE)`) rather than turning it into a two-step process as I did, but memory is confusing and a more informative message could have prevented a few of the rabbit holes I went down before this all made sense)

Thanks for considering this!

title: The privacy concern
description:
In the README, the main goal that is mentioned for the package is to reduce the size.  My main motivation for removing training data from model objects are privacy issues: I want to be able to publish the model without publishing the training data.  (Of course, the model itself depends on the training data, so a full separation of the model from the training data might not be possible, but at least I want to make sure that my model does not contain an explicit copy of the training data.)

Would it make sense to expand the scope of the package to address this goal?

Sometimes privacy and size constraints may lead to different approaches:

- If I care about privacy, I might decide to only keep those parts of the model that I am sure that I will use later.  That is, I need a list of components which I cannot drop.
- If I worry about size, I might decide to only drop those parts of the model that I surely don't need.  That is, I would work with a list of components that I can safely drop without reducing the desired functionality.

What are your thoughts on this?

title: axe_data() method for xgb.Booster objects
description:
It is [documented](https://butcher.tidymodels.org/articles/available-axe-methods.html) that the axe_data() method does not work for xgb.Booster objects. (See related discussion [here](https://github.com/tidymodels/butcher/issues/147).) This is a major problem for those working in industry because:

* xgb.Booster are perhaps the most popular machine learning model, at least for numeric data, in industry.

* Professional users often work with very large amounts of data.

* Professional users often create many models and/or use model ensembles.

Without being able to remove the data associated with each model object using axe_data(), we end up with numerous model objects, each with an entire copy of the original data set. This makes a tidymodels approach unworkable, which makes me sad. I, at least, have no choice but to use xgb.train() directly.

title: Using {xgboost} predict after `butcher()`
description:
## Problem

After saving [and then reading/using] a {butcher}ed xgboost model, the `predict()` function no longer works. I've provided a {reprex} example below. I believe butcher doesn't delete the model reference, so once you save/read via `readRDS()` and/or restart the R session `predict()` no longer works (because the reference has finally been deleted). This explains why the tests didn't pick this up either.

``` r
## load xgboost
library(xgboost)

## train a model
xgb_mod <- xgboost(
  data = as.matrix(mtcars[, -6]),
  label = mtcars[["vs"]],
  nrounds = 10)
#> [1]  train-rmse:0.358817 
#> [2]  train-rmse:0.257504 
#> [3]  train-rmse:0.184800 
#> [4]  train-rmse:0.132626 
#> [5]  train-rmse:0.095183 
#> [6]  train-rmse:0.068313 
#> [7]  train-rmse:0.049029 
#> [8]  train-rmse:0.035189 
#> [9]  train-rmse:0.025256 
#> [10] train-rmse:0.018127

## predict like normal
predict(xgb_mod, as.matrix(mtcars[, -6]))
#>  [1] 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.98128045
#>  [7] 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.01765314
#> [13] 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.98128045
#> [19] 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314
#> [25] 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.01765314
#> [31] 0.01765314 0.98128045

## butcher
xgb_mod <- butcher::butcher(xgb_mod)

## predict again works like normal
predict(xgb_mod, as.matrix(mtcars[, -6]))
#>  [1] 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.98128045
#>  [7] 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.01765314
#> [13] 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.98128045
#> [19] 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.01765314 0.01765314
#> [25] 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.98128045 0.01765314 0.01765314
#> [31] 0.01765314 0.98128045

## save model object
saveRDS(xgb_mod, "xgb_mod.rds")

## now read model object
xgb_mod <- readRDS("xgb_mod.rds")

## now it doesn't work
predict(xgb_mod, as.matrix(mtcars[, -6]))
#> Error in xgb.Booster.handle(modelfile = object$raw): AssertError:read can not have position excceed buffer length
```

<sup>Created on 2020-01-31 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

## Solution

I came up with the following solution, which uses `xgboost::xgb.load()` to convert the (raw) model object into a slimmed down xgb model. As the reprex shows below, this would still provide a significant reduction in memory!


``` r
## load xgboost
library(xgboost)

## train a model
xgb_mod <- xgboost(
  data = as.matrix(mtcars[, -6]),
  label = mtcars[["vs"]],
  nrounds = 10)
#> [1]  train-rmse:0.358817 
#> [2]  train-rmse:0.257504 
#> [3]  train-rmse:0.184800 
#> [4]  train-rmse:0.132626 
#> [5]  train-rmse:0.095183 
#> [6]  train-rmse:0.068313 
#> [7]  train-rmse:0.049029 
#> [8]  train-rmse:0.035189 
#> [9]  train-rmse:0.025256 
#> [10] train-rmse:0.018127

## save the model
xgb_mod_raw <- xgb_mod$raw

## restore the model using xgb.load directly
xgb_mod2 <- xgboost::xgb.load(xgb_mod_raw)

## and save/read prior to xgb.load
saveRDS(xgb_mod_raw, "xgb_mod_raw")
xgb_mod3 <- xgboost::xgb.load(readRDS("xgb_mod_raw"))

## compare sizes
object.size(xgb_mod)
#> 88552 bytes
object.size(xgb_mod2)
#> 3912 bytes
object.size(xgb_mod3)
#> 3912 bytes

## validate
identical(
  predict(xgb_mod, as.matrix(mtcars[, -6])),
  predict(xgb_mod2, as.matrix(mtcars[, -6])),
  predict(xgb_mod2, as.matrix(mtcars[, -6]))
)
#> [1] TRUE
```

``` r
library(butcher)
```

```r
  step_normalize(starts_with("Petal.")) %>%
  step_BoxCox(starts_with("Sepal."))
```

The proposed implementation is quite simple, if I'm not missing anything:

```r
axe_fitted.recipe <- function(x, verbose = FALSE, ...) {
  old <- x
  x$template <- x$template[integer(), ]

  add_butcher_attributes(
    x,
    old,
    verbose = verbose
  )
}
```

title: Missing `axe_env.step_normalize`
description:
It seems as those the size of recipes can grow very quickly when saving the same exact recipe within vs. outside of a function. This is true even after using `butcher` on the recipes themselves. On some examples I've worked out with large datasets inside of a function, the difference can be ~ 600Kb vs. 30 Gb. This issue is related to an [issue here](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/503) but it doesn't quite seem like butcher entirely fixes this issue specifically when saving recipes inside of a function.

Here is a simple reproducible example using the iris data set. 
```
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
library(butcher)
library(readr)
library(fs)

### Save Recipe Outside of Function
rec <- 
  recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_pca(all_numeric()) %>% 
  prep()

rec <- butcher(rec)
write_rds(rec, 'recipe_outside_of_function.rds')

### Save Recipe inside of Function
my_function <- function() {
  rec <- 
    recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris) %>% 
    step_normalize(all_numeric()) %>% 
    step_pca(all_numeric()) %>% 
    prep()
  
  rec <- butcher(rec)
  write_rds(rec, 'recipe_inside_of_function.rds')
}
my_function()


### Save Recipe inside of Funtion
my_function2 <- function() {
  a <- iris
  b <- iris
  c <- iris
  rec <- 
    recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris) %>% 
    step_normalize(all_numeric()) %>% 
    step_pca(all_numeric()) %>% 
    prep()
  
  rec <- butcher(rec)
  write_rds(rec, 'recipe_inside_of_function_more_stuff.rds')
}
my_function2()

files <- c('recipe_outside_of_function.rds',
           'recipe_inside_of_function.rds',
           'recipe_inside_of_function_more_stuff.rds')

### Print File Sizes
file_size(files)           
#> 18.7K 30K 47.1K
```

As we can see, the same exact recipe, even after being butchered, is different sizes on disk. Furthermore, the more stuff we do inside of the function, the larger the recipe seems to grow, even if such steps are completely unrelated to the recipe itself. Thanks for the help and let me know if anything else can be provided in this example!

title: Generic function help files
description: To go along with #4, we need a way to make the help page for lm specific methods more discoverable. Right now, if you have the package installed, you'd have to do `?axe_env.lm`. But that actually doesn't work, because if you have the package installed the only thing that you really can see is `butcher::axe_env`, not `butcher::axe_env.lm`. To see the lm specific page you'd have to do `?butcher:::axe_env.lm` with the triple colon. This will be difficult for users. To make it easier to find, I think we can take a page out of the generics + broom playbook. In a fresh R session, try calling `?broom::tidy` without loading broom. You should be taken to a page where you can click through to `tidy` from generics. At the bottom of that next page you should see a `Methods` section that shouldn't have any methods in it. Now `library(broom)`. And call `?broom::tidy` again and click through to that page. It should be populated with links to all kinds of broom model specific help pages. This is _dynamic documentation_, and we might be able to do a similar thing here. Doing `?axe_env` would take you to a page that would dynamically link to all of the loaded model specific `axe_env` help pages. To do this, we will probably have to copy the generics function for this, in this file. I don't think we should put all of the `axe_*()` functions in the generics package, which would be the normal approach to add a new common generic function: https://github.com/r-lib/generics/blob/master/R/docs.R To make the dynamic docs work, you do this in the roxygen help files, but it will be specific to the `axe_env` generic, not `explain`, and it won't be `generics:::` but probably `butcher:::` https://github.com/r-lib/generics/blob/c15ac433450078b581cdfa5d9a3c10797f3a3fd5/R/explain.R#L7

title: `sysdata.rda` thoughts
description:
I'm not entirely sure what the right approach should be here, but I _think_ that rather than having 1 sysdata.rda file, I would rather take the readxl approach where the data files are all stored in `inst/extdata/` and then a helper is provided to load the examples.

https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/master/R/example.R
https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/tree/master/inst/extdata

The `inst/extdata/` directory is blessed by CRAN
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Data-in-packages

As it currently stands, the issues with the sysdata.rda approach are:

- It is hard to tell at a glance exactly what example data sets are there
- These are actually all _internal only_. So you can't use them in examples. For example, this won't actually work `axe_misc(glmnet_multi)` (I'm fairly certain). However, I'm not sure you'd actually want to use them in examples. Rather, you might want to actually show examples of creating the objects with the modeling functions, and then pruning them. This gives a clearer picture of how the package will be used.

I _do_ really like the fact that there is a script that generates the test data files.

So here are my thoughts:

- Create an `inst/extdata/` folder. This will be included in the R package.
- Create a `inst/extdata-scripts/` folder. This won't be bundled with the R package, so use `usethis::use_build_ignore("inst/extdata-scripts")` to add it do the `.Rbuildignore`. (I think that should work)
- I would have 1 file per data set in `extdata-scripts/` that generates 1 dataset in `extdata/`. They should have matching file names. 
- Create a helper like readxl that can read in the datasets when requested.
- Use this helper in tests, but maybe not in examples. In examples, as mentioned above i think it would be most clear if we could actually `library()` the relevant package and show off the methods after using the package to create a model object.
- I am unsure if the helper should be exported at the current moment.

I'm going to open another issue about what I think the examples sections could look like.

title: Model specific help files
description: I think it might be useful to have the help files be "model specific" as well. So, what I am suggesting is that `lm` would have one help file that would have `axe_env.lm`, `axe_call.lm` and so on all documented in one place. That would allow you to document exactly what `axe_misc.lm` does, right in the lm specific help doc. Doing this is a bit of a trick, because you have to really know how roxygen comments work. It looks something like this: ```r #' Axing an lm #' #' This is where all of the lm specific documentation lies #' #' #' @name axe-lm NULL #' @rdname axe-lm #' @export axe_call.lm <- function(x, ...) { x$call <- call("dummy_call") x } #' @rdname axe-lm #' @export axe_env.lm <- function(x, ...) { # Environment in terms x$terms <- axe_env(x$terms, ...) # Environment in model attributes(x$model)$terms <- axe_env(attributes(x$model)$terms, ...) x } ``` This is also where I would actually use `lm()` to create a lm object, and then you could call all of the relevant axing functions on it to show what it does. This is slightly more complicated when a package is required to call the model (`lm()` comes with base R). Like for flexsurv, to be able to run `library(flexsurv)` in the examples section, you have to have flexsurv as a Suggests. I am still not sure if this is what we will do in the long run, but we can give it a try for now.

description:
I just hit this interesting scenario where `butcher()` gives a larger object than we started with, so we get this `"No memory released"` warning.

``` r
library(earth)
library(butcher)

earth.mod <- earth(Volume ~ ., data = trees)

butcher(earth.mod)
#> ✖ No memory released. Do not butcher.
#> Selected 4 of 5 terms, and 2 of 2 predictors
#> Termination condition: RSq changed by less than 0.001 at 5 terms
#> Importance: Girth, Height
#> Number of terms at each degree of interaction: 1 3 (additive model)
#> GCV 11.25439    RSS 209.1139    GRSq 0.959692    RSq 0.9742029

axe_call(earth.mod)
#> ✔ Memory released: '144 B'
#> ✖ Disabled: `summary`, `update`
#> Selected 4 of 5 terms, and 2 of 2 predictors
#> Termination condition: RSq changed by less than 0.001 at 5 terms
#> Importance: Girth, Height
#> Number of terms at each degree of interaction: 1 3 (additive model)
#> GCV 11.25439    RSS 209.1139    GRSq 0.959692    RSq 0.9742029
```

<sup>Created on 2019-07-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

Upon looking into this, `axe_data()` for `.earth` does:

```r
function(x, verbose = TRUE, ...) {
  old <- x
  x$x <- data.frame(NA)
  x$y <- numeric(0)

  add_butcher_attributes(x, old,
                         disabled = c("update"),
                         verbose = verbose)
}
```

but `$x` and `$y` don't exist in `earth.mod` to start with, so this ends up _adding_ memory rather than removing it! This is because `keepxy = FALSE` by default in `earth()`.

I think you might want to have a function called `exchange(x, what, with)` that would replace the object at location `x[[what]]` _only_ if something actually exists there already. Then you would use it like:

```r
function(x, verbose = TRUE, ...) {
  old <- x
  x <- exchange(x, "x", data.frame(NA))
  x <- exchange(x, "y", numeric(0))
  
  add_butcher_attributes(
    x, 
    old,
    disabled = c("update"),
    verbose = verbose
  )
}
```

title: Consider whether axe generics should be moved to `generics`
Parsnip now uses the formula interface for earth()
description:
Part of this parsnip commit changed from using the xy interface of earth() to the formula interface https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/commit/3a3c1341ea20784b179165dcc563fd498eda37e8#diff-bd710ae9957786d392ecee8bc45e2ddf3761ca605ddbc4fd7bc18886840b4254

This means that `earth(keepxy = TRUE)` now retains `data` rather than `x` and `y`. Currently, butcher only knows how to butcher `x` and `y`, and the tests in butcher that compare against parsnip also expect `x` to have been there and now fail because of the parsnip update (we didnt get notified about any cran failures because these tests have `skip_on_cran()`).

I'm prepping a PR to fix this and a few other test failures
